What is the optimal strategy, and roughly what success probability does it achieve as the candidate pool grows large?
choices: Reject roughly the first 37% automatically, then hire the next candidate who beats everyone seen so far — this succeeds about 37% of the time
Interview everyone, then go back and hire the best one — this succeeds 100% of the time
Always hire the very first candidate — this succeeds 100% of the time
Reject the first half automatically, then hire the next one who beats everyone seen so far — this succeeds about 50% of the time

questions.q: You're given a sealed envelope containing an unknown amount of money X. You're told a second sealed envelope contains either half or double of X, each equally likely. Before opening either, you're offered the chance to switch. An argument claims the expected value of the other envelope is 1.25X, so you should always switch. What is actually true?
choices: You should switch only if X happens to be an even number
You should never switch, since the envelopes are identical in appearance
The argument is correct — you should always switch to gain 25% in expectation
The argument is flawed — it treats the fixed unknown amount in your envelope as if it were a random variable, so there is no expected gain from switching

questions.q: Buses arrive at a stop according to a Poisson process, averaging one bus every 10 minutes (so some gaps are longer than average and some shorter, but they average 10 minutes). If you arrive at a uniformly random time, what is your expected waiting time for the next bus?
choices: It cannot be determined without more information
10 minutes — the same as the average gap, due to the inspection paradox

questions.q: Three doors hide a car and two goats. You pick Door 1. Unlike the classic Monty Hall setup, this host does NOT know what's behind the doors — he opens one of the other two doors uniformly at random, and it happens to reveal a goat. Should you switch to the remaining door, and what is your probability of winning the car if you do?
choices: Switch; the probability of winning is 2/3, exactly as in the classic Monty Hall problem
Switch; the probability of winning is now 1/2
It cannot be determined without knowing which door the host prefers
Stay; the probability of winning is 2/3

questions.q: Let A be the event 'a stock's price rises next week' and B be the event 'the stock's price rises next week AND its trading volume also increases.' Which of these is necessarily true, regardless of how A and B are correlated?
choices: P(B) ≤ P(A), since B is a more specific, conjoined version of A
P(B) ≥ P(A), since B contains more information
P(B) > P(A), since adding a plausible detail makes the combined scenario more likely

questions.q: A small college has 10 classes: nine classes have 10 students each, and one large lecture has 100 students. The registrar computes the average class size as (9×10 + 100) ÷ 10 = 19 students. If instead you ask a randomly chosen student how many people are in their class and average all the answers, what do you get?
choices: About 100, the size of the largest class
About 57, much higher, because far more students sit in the large class
About 19, the same as the registrar's figure

questions.q: A large hospital averages about 45 births a day; a small hospital averages about 15 births a day. Over a year, which hospital is more likely to record a day on which more than 60% of the births were boys?
choices: The large hospital, because it records more births overall
Both equally likely, since the sex ratio is 50/50 regardless of sample size
It cannot be determined without knowing the exact daily counts
The small hospital, because smaller samples fluctuate further from 50%

choices: HT takes longer on average (expected 6 flips vs 4)
